title: Continuous prefetch mosaic admission and tail-window optimizer for latency stability
creator: Jordan Kim
description:
Summary:
We need a continuous-batching enhancement that reduces tail latency variability without sacrificing throughput or token-cost efficiency. This ticket builds a runtime admission controller and a lightweight prefetch/kernels "mosaic" that can select different execution kernels and attention paths within a single admission window based on per-request token distribution and prefix KV hints. The goal is to stabilize 99th/99.9th percentile latency for mixed-length traffic (2-1024 tokens) while keeping average token cost within 3% of current baseline.

Background and motivation:
- Production traffic shows heavy variance: short steady queries alongside long-generation chat sessions, and a non-trivial fraction of bursty prefill requests that create stragglers.
- Current continuous-batcher groups by arrival time and approximate seq-len; kernel routing is per-batch and sometimes forces suboptimal kernel choices causing tail spikes when a misfit request enters a batch mid-window.
- We previously implemented kernel hints and profiling (see ENG-31247, ENG-46210) but still observe tail percentiles when attention memory or quantization path mismatches occur.

Proposed approach and components:
1) Tail-window admission controller: a sliding micro-window (25ms default) that maintains low-latency "tail watermarks" per GPU worker. Instead of fixed-size windows we use dynamic expiry and a soft-grace quota to prevent long requests from monopolizing admission. This controller exposes a small budget for speculative prefetch slots.
2) Prefetch-aware weighting: when admission sees a mixture of short and long requests, the controller earmarks speculative KV prefetch slots for long-prefill candidates and limits slot consumption by short decodes using per-tenant weights.
3) Mosaic kernel selection: rather than a single kernel per batch, we enable intra-batch kernel mosaicing: fast lightweight kernel for short sequences (FP16/fused attention), fall-back kernel for long sequences (chunked attention / memory-efficient path), and a hybrid quantized path for eligible models. Kernels are selected per-request at admission using a compact feature vector (seq_len, kv_size_hint, quantization_hint, latency_budget).
4) Prefill-decode scheduling handshake: introduce a two-phase handshake where prefill requests can mark themselves as "deferred-prefill" to be admitted into the mosaic with a higher tolerance for batching delay in exchange for lower decode-time contention.

Metrics and success criteria:
- Primary: 99th percentile latency reduction of at least 20% on mixed workloads, 99.9th percentile reduced by >=15% compared to baseline.
- Secondary: Throughput (tokens/sec) drop <=3%, average token compute cost delta <=+3%.
- Operational: No increase in GPU OOM incidents, no regression for dedicated customers on pinned capacity.

Implementation plan (milestones):
- Spike (1 week): microbench harness to simulate mixed traffic and prototype the tail-window controller and the mosaic router in user-space. Produce a latency/throughput matrix. (Owner: Ava)
- Engine change (2 weeks): implement admission controller in the runtime loop, expose per-worker tail watermark metrics and a sampled admission trace. Add in-kernel hooks to support two kernels per batch. (Owner: backend team)
- Kernel integration (2 weeks): integrate the 'fast' and 'fall-back' kernels and add a lightweight kernel decision function. Add unit tests for kernel path correctness. (Owner: kernel/opt team)
- Canary (1 week): rollout to canary pool, collect dashboards for 50k QPS synthetic plus 10% production mirrored traffic.
- Rollout and tuning (2 weeks): iterate thresholds, adjust mosaic ratio and prefetch budgets, finalize runbook.

Trade-offs and risks:
- Complexity: Intra-batch kernel mosaicing increases scheduling complexity and can complicate failure modes. We mitigate by limiting mosaics to at most 2 kernel types per batch and by instrumenting a per-batch fallback path.
- Cost: Some additional wasted cycles from prefetch speculation; budgeted to be small and tunable.
- Correctness: Different kernels must produce bit-compatible logits; we'll require conformance tests and deterministic seeds for smoke tests.

Testing and validation:
- Unit tests for kernel-decision logic, admission quotas, and handshake states.
- Integration tests using the perf-harness with traffic shapes: short-only, long-only, mixed (60/40), and bursty arrival with Poisson bursts.
- A/B canary comparing latency percentiles and token-cost on production-similar load.

Rollout plan and observability:
- Add metrics: tail_window_fill, mosaic_ratio, kernel_switch_rate, speculative_prefetch_hits, per-request kernel_tag.
- Dashboards: runtime/continuous-batching/mosaic and runtime/continuous-batching/tail-window. Attach alerts for tail_window_fill > 0.8 sustained for 1m.
- Runbook: immediate rollback flag in canary if 99.9th increases by >5% or OOM events spike.

Open decisions:
- Default micro-window size (25ms vs 50ms) and how to tier by hardware generation.
- Whether to expose mosaic controls to Dedicated tenants (initially off by default).

Artifacts and links:
- Design doc (Confluence): https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RUNTIME/Mosaic+Admission+Design
- Spike notebook and logs (Drive): https://drive.redwood.ai/drive/folders/1aMosaicSpike
- Benchmark harness (GitHub): https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime-perf-harness/pull/142
- Canary PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1997

Next steps:
- Begin spike this sprint; schedule sync with kernel team and PM for exact canary host selection.
acceptance_criteria: Tail-window controller implemented and emitting metrics
Mosaic kernel selection reachable in admission path with unit tests
Canary run shows >=20% improvement at 99th on mixed traffic or clear mitigation plan
No regressions in throughput >3% and no increase in OOM incidents
